column2: Persistent authentication to many systems, autonomous execution without review, and a natural-language interface with no reliable sanitization.
Language models have no equivalent of SQL parameterization; the same parsing that follows real instructions also follows injected ones.
An attacker plants instructions in content the agent handles normally, such as an email. No access to the user's systems is needed.
Instructions hidden in white text, HTML comments or metadata of pages the agent reads during research.
Instructions embedded in a third-party API response. Dangerous because tool output is often treated as trusted.
An instruction planted in content later loaded as context, including the agent's own memory. It persists across sessions.
A SOUL.md rule that refuses requests from any source to adopt a different persona or rule set.
A vulnerability that let arbitrary websites hijack agent sessions. Broad permissions, no gates and no external-content rule enabled it; the fix needed all three.
A benign skill gathers installs, then a later update adds a malicious payload while SKILL.md stays unchanged.
Read every execution file, find all network calls, check filesystem and environment-variable access, and verify the publisher.
Pin each skill version and turn off auto-update. Updates are not re-reviewed, so diff and review before upgrading.
A malicious skill reaches every system the agent can reach and runs as code on the host, with no model reasoning step.
Skills granted more permissions than their function needs. Fix by splitting a skill into permission tiers and gating sends.
The agent takes consequential actions without human oversight. Primary control: confirmation requirements in AGENTS.md.
Corrupting memory stores to change future behavior. Control: no memory writes while processing external content.
Missing records to reconstruct an incident. Log tool calls with inputs and outputs plus transcripts, outside the workspace, for 90+ days.
A compromised orchestrator passes its trusted authority down to sub-agents. Sub-agents should not hold permissions the orchestrator lacks.
A too-short heartbeat interval combined with large context and a premium model produces a large idle cost.
Granting tokens broader scopes than needed, such as full Gmail access when gmail.readonly would do.
How openclaw.json references environment variables. Literal credential values never belong in that file.
Behavioral, permission, access control and operational. Each layer assumes the others may fail.
Messages from non-allowlisted accounts get no reply at all, because any reply reveals that the bot exists.
Stop the agent first, then assess external impact, then reconstruct what happened. Do not restart before fixing the root cause.
Behavioral gap, prompt injection, permission misconfiguration, and supply chain compromise. The category determines the fix.
Run any trading skill against a simulated brokerage account with the full test battery before switching to live credentials.
